job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — 10,000-ton threshold.** The definition covers only recovery of “more than” 10,000 metric tons, so recovery of exactly 10,000 tons or less by a vessel is outside the prohibition.

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — Fleet-splitting loophole.** Because the threshold applies “by a single vessel,” an operator could divide recovery among multiple vessels, each remaining below 10,001 tons, even if the fleet collectively recovers far more.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Non-vessel recovery.** Mining performed by platforms, remotely operated systems, subsea installations, or other equipment not legally considered a “vessel” may fall outside subparagraph (A).

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — Uncertain attribution among vessels.** The bill does not say which vessel is deemed to recover minerals when one vessel controls subsea equipment and another lifts, stores, processes, or transports the material.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Per year” is undefined.** It is unclear whether the threshold applies by calendar year, fiscal year, license year, or a rolling 12-month period, permitting operations to structure recovery around whichever interpretation is most favorable.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — Quantity measurement is unspecified.** The bill does not prescribe where, when, or how tonnage is measured, including whether it means wet weight, dry weight, material lifted from the seabed, material retained after processing, or saleable mineral output.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth boundary.** Mining at exactly 200 meters is excluded because the definition requires depths “greater than 200 meters”; operations in shallower water are also unaffected regardless of environmental impact.

8. **Section 2(1)(A) — Depth measurement is ambiguous.** The bill supplies no datum or method for measuring depth and does not address tides, seabed variation across a collection area, or an operation spanning both sides of the 200-meter boundary.

9. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Recovery” is undefined.** The term could mean initial disturbance, lifting material from the seabed, bringing it aboard, retaining it, or completing processing, creating uncertainty for tests, temporary collection, rejected material, and material transferred at sea.

10. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Other mineral resources” is indeterminate.** The phrase could sweep in virtually every seabed mineral or, under a narrower reading based on context, only resources similar to polymetallic nodules; the bill gives no limiting principle.

11. **Section 2(1)(B) — Unidentified “Secretary.”** The Act never defines “Secretary,” so it is unclear which Cabinet officer can designate additional activities, particularly because section 6 separately and expressly refers to the Secretary of State.

12. **Section 2(1)(B) — No designation procedure.** The bill provides no rulemaking, notice, hearing, evidence, timing, publication, or judicial-review procedure for a determination that an activity presents comparable risks.

13. **Section 2(1)(B) — Vague comparison standard.** “Risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to” subparagraph (A) does not identify relevant harms, probability, geographic scale, duration, or a baseline operation against which comparability is measured.

14. **Section 2(1)(B) — Uncertain prospective effect.** The bill does not state whether a Secretarial determination operates only prospectively or can convert previously lawful conduct into a civil or criminal violation after the conduct occurs.

15. **Section 2(1)(B) — Overbreadth and possible delegation problem.** “Any activity” could include research, fishing, cable work, or navigation rather than mining, while the absence of an intelligible limiting standard creates vagueness and nondelegation concerns, especially given criminal penalties.

16. **Section 2(2) — Individuals omitted from “U.S. person.”** The definition includes U.S. citizens but not lawful permanent residents, U.S. nationals who are not citizens, or other noncitizens domiciled in the United States; those individuals are covered abroad only if they are presently “in the United States.”

17. **Section 2(2) — Business forms omitted or uncertain.** Partnerships, trusts, joint ventures, unincorporated associations, and potentially limited liability companies are not corporations and therefore may not be “U.S. persons.”

18. **Section 2(2) — Territorial and federal entities omitted.** Corporations organized under District of Columbia, territorial, tribal, or federal law are not plainly corporations organized “under the laws of a State.”

19. **Section 2(2) — Foreign-subsidiary loophole.** A foreign-organized subsidiary is not a U.S. person even if wholly owned or controlled by a U.S. corporation; the bill contains no ownership, control, agency, or anti-evasion rule.

20. **Section 2(3) — Registry threshold mismatch.** Only vessels over 5,000 gross tons must register, although a smaller vessel can recover more than 10,000 metric tons per year and trigger section 3; conversely, a large vessel may have to register without doing prohibited mining.

21. **Section 2(3) — “Gross tons” is unclear.** Gross tonnage is ordinarily a measure of enclosed volume rather than weight, and the bill does not identify the tonnage convention or certificate to use.

22. **Section 2(3) — “Equipped for recovery” is manipulable.** The bill does not address modular, leased, detachable, or temporarily removed equipment, allowing uncertainty over when a vessel becomes or ceases to be covered.

23. **Section 3(a) — Territorial scope is undefined.** “In the United States” does not expressly address U.S. territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the outer continental shelf, U.S.-flag vessels, possessions, or conduct partly inside and partly outside U.S. jurisdiction.

24. **Section 3(a) — Indirect participation is not addressed.** “Engage in” does not clearly cover financing, insuring, owning, directing, contracting for, processing, transporting, purchasing, or selling minerals recovered by another entity.

25. **Section 3(a) — Below-threshold mining remains lawful.** Despite the Act’s title, section 3 prohibits only the specially defined “commercial deep seabed mining,” leaving recovery outside the numerical, depth, vessel, and Secretarial-determination criteria untouched.

26. **Section 3(b) — Exploration-license grandfather is extraordinarily broad.** The exception permits “mining” under a pre-enactment exploration license, effectively allowing commercial production under an instrument that need not itself be a mining license.

27. **Section 3(b) — Issuing authority is unspecified.** The bill does not say whether the qualifying exploration license must be issued by NOAA, another U.S. agency, the International Seabed Authority, a foreign government, or any other entity.

28. **Section 3(b) — No limits on grandfathered operations.** The exception contains no restriction based on licensed area, production volume, environmental conditions, vessel, operator, assignment, renewal, amendment, or license expiration.

29. **Section 3(b) — Transfer and expansion are unresolved.** Nothing expressly prevents a pre-enactment license from being sold, assigned, renewed, amended, or used by affiliates after enactment, potentially extending the exception to new parties and greatly enlarged operations.

30. **Section 3(b) — “Conducted under” is vague.** The phrase does not establish how closely mining must conform to a license’s terms or whether ancillary, experimental, or geographically related activity qualifies.

31. **Section 3(c) — Environmental-assessment loophole.** The exemption is based solely on the activity’s “purpose” and has no approval, protocol, tonnage, duration, disposition, or independent-verification requirement, allowing substantial recovery to be characterized as environmental assessment.

32. **Section 3(c) — Mixed-purpose activities.** The bill does not say whether the exemption applies when environmental assessment is one purpose but mineral recovery, technology testing, or commercial preparation is another.

33. **Section 3(c) — No restriction on use or sale of recovered material.** Material collected during an asserted environmental assessment is not required to be returned, destroyed, limited in quantity, or withheld from commercial sale.

34. **Section 4(a) — “Operator” is undefined.** Ownership, bareboat charter, technical management, navigation, and control of mining equipment may rest with different entities, leaving it unclear who must register.

35. **Section 4(a) — Registry jurisdiction is overbroad or incomplete.** Read literally, “each covered vessel” includes foreign vessels and operations with no U.S. nexus; if an implicit jurisdictional limitation is assumed, the bill never specifies what it is.

36. **Section 4(a) — No registration mechanics.** The provision establishes no deadline, application content, renewal obligation, registration standard, denial authority, or requirement that NOAA establish a registry before operations begin.

37. **Section 4(b) — Reporting duties are indeterminate.** The bill does not define the quarterly periods, submission deadlines, required measurements, recordkeeping rules, reporting format, or treatment of quarters before registration.

38. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry and reporting are unenforceable.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, so failure to register, report, or report accurately under section 4 carries no express civil or criminal penalty.

39. **Section 4(b) — Certification has no stated consequence.** The bill does not prescribe certification language or expressly impose liability for a false certification, leaving enforcement to generally applicable statutes whose coverage may depend on the circumstances.

40. **Section 5(a) — Penalty timing conflicts with the effective date.** Civil penalties purport to apply to violations occurring on or after enactment, but section 8 says the Act does not take effect until 180 days later; there can be no operative section 3 violation during that interval unless section 8 is disregarded.

41. **Section 5(a) — No enforcement machinery.** The bill does not identify the enforcing agency, adjudicator, assessment process, venue, limitations period, collection authority, or factors governing the amount of a civil penalty.

42. **Section 5(a) — Daily violations are undefined.** It is unclear whether a violation occurs every day a voyage continues, only on days material is physically recovered, separately for each vessel or person, or separately for each prohibited act.

43. **Section 5(a) — Penalty ceiling permits nominal penalties.** “Not more than” $1,000,000 establishes no minimum and supplies no penalty factors, potentially allowing penalties too small to deter a profitable operation.

44. **Section 5(b) — Criminal scope is uncertain.** “Willfully” is undefined, including whether prosecutors must prove knowledge of the law, knowledge of the facts that cross the threshold, or merely intentional operation; this is especially problematic given the bill’s ambiguous measurements and Secretarial designations.

45. **Section 5(b) — No treatment of organizational responsibility.** The bill does not specify when a corporation, parent company, officer, employee, vessel master, contractor, or beneficial owner is criminally responsible for organizational conduct.

46. **Section 6 — “Seek to negotiate” is weak and unenforceable.** The Secretary of State need only attempt negotiations within 18 months and is not required to conclude, sign, submit, or obtain ratification of an agreement.

47. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” prohibitions are undefined.** The provision supplies no standard for equivalence and does not require an agreement to reproduce the Act’s jurisdiction, thresholds, exceptions, enforcement, or duration.

48. **Sections 6 and 7(b) — International-agreement timing conflict.** An agreement negotiated under section 6 could impose obligations extending beyond the Act’s ten-year sunset, but the bill does not address withdrawal, termination, or the relationship between those obligations and expiration of domestic law.

49. **Section 7(a) — No National Academies report mechanism.** The bill neither commissions nor funds a report, specifies its scope or timing, nor identifies who must request it, so the statutory route to ending the prohibition may never become usable.

50. **Section 7(a) — “Acting on a report” is indefinite.** The bill does not require a current, bill-specific, or favorable report, meaning virtually any relevant National Academies report might be asserted as sufficient—or rejected as insufficient.

51. **Section 7(a) — “Without serious harm” is undefined.** The provision supplies no definition of harm, seriousness, affected ecosystem, acceptable risk, geographic scope, or time horizon for Congress’s finding.

52. **Section 7(a) — Joint-resolution procedure is missing.** There is no prescribed text, introduction mechanism, committee deadline, expedited procedure, or statement of whether a joint resolution must be presented to the President in the ordinary constitutional manner.

53. **Section 7(a) — Effect of an early finding is unclear.** A qualifying resolution ends “the prohibition in section 3,” but the bill does not state whether the definitions, registry, reporting provisions, penalties, and international-negotiation directive remain operative.

54. **Section 7(a) and (b) — Conflicting duration rules.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition remains until Congress makes the required finding, while subsection (b) terminates the entire Act after ten years even if Congress never makes that finding; the sunset likely controls, but the provisions are facially inconsistent.

55. **Section 7(b) — Automatic reopening without a safety finding.** After ten years, the Act expires regardless of environmental evidence, so mining can resume without the National Academies report or congressional finding contemplated by subsection (a).

56. **Section 7(b) — Effect on pending liabilities is unstated.** The bill does not say what happens to pending investigations, penalties, prosecutions, reporting duties, or accrued violations when the Act sunsets, leaving reliance on general federal saving principles and inviting litigation.

57. **Section 8 — Delayed implementation without transition rules.** The Act provides no rules for operations begun, quantities recovered, licenses issued, vessels registered, or Secretarial determinations made during the 180-day interval between enactment and effectiveness.

58. **Sections 3(b) and 8 — License cutoff precedes operative prohibition.** A license must be issued before enactment to qualify for grandfathering, even though the prohibition begins 180 days later, creating an unexplained class of licenses issued during the interim that are valid when issued but unprotected once the Act takes effect.

59. **Act-wide — No coordination with existing law.** The bill does not explain how it interacts with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act, Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, existing permits, international licenses, federal environmental statutes, treaty obligations, or state law.

60. **Act-wide — No implementing-rule authority.** No agency is expressly authorized or required to issue regulations resolving measurement, jurisdiction, exemptions, registration, reporting, enforcement, or evidentiary questions.

61. **Act-wide — No anti-evasion or aggregation provision.** The bill does not aggregate affiliated companies, coordinated vessels, sequential operators, license transfers, or related voyages, making its vessel-specific and entity-specific limits particularly susceptible to formal restructuring.

62. **Act-wide — No severability clause.** If a court invalidates a central feature—particularly the open-ended Secretarial designation authority—it is uncertain whether the numerical prohibition, exceptions, registry, or penalty provisions would remain in force.
